reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a naevus comedonicus, grouped dilated follicular openings plugged with keratin resembling clustered comedones, in a segmental Blaschko-linear pattern, together with extracutaneous anomalies
It is a mosaic disorder, with post-zygotic activating NEK9 variants reported, and shares the epidermal-naevus spectrum classification
The naevus represents a hamartoma of the pilosebaceous unit rather than true acne, though it may become inflamed with cysts and abscesses
Central nervous system associations include seizures, developmental delay and structural brain anomalies
Skeletal defects such as scoliosis, vertebral and limb anomalies, and ipsilateral bony changes may occur
Ocular associations such as cataract and other anterior-segment anomalies warrant ophthalmology review
Management is generic and largely symptomatic: keratolytics and topical retinoids for the naevus, treatment of secondary infection, and surgery for troublesome or extensive lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Naevus comedonicus syndrome arises from a post-zygotic mosaic variant, with activating NEK9 variants described, affecting a clone of follicular keratinocytes during embryogenesis. This produces a hamartomatous malformation of the pilosebaceous unit in which rudimentary follicles fail to form normal hair and sebaceous structures and instead retain keratin, giving the characteristic comedo-like plugs distributed along the lines of Blaschko. Secondary inflammation, cyst formation and bacterial infection can complicate the lesion. When the mosaic clone extends to neuroectodermal, ocular and skeletal progenitors, the associated central nervous system, ocular and skeletal malformations of the syndrome develop.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated naevus comedonicus without systemic features
Dilated pore of Winer and comedonal cysts
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm the follicular hamartoma
MRI of the brain where seizures or developmental delay are present
Spinal and limb radiographs for scoliosis and skeletal anomalies
Ophthalmological assessment for cataract and anterior-segment defects
Swabs and cultures where secondary infection or abscess is suspected
Molecular analysis of lesional tissue for mosaic NEK9 variants where available
redFlags: Progressive neurological deficit or developmental regression
Recurrent abscess or deep infection within the naevus
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous lesion is benign but often cosmetically and symptomatically troublesome, and prognosis overall depends on the severity of any neurological, ocular or skeletal involvement, which determines the need for long-term multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Mistaking the naevus for ordinary acne and missing the segmental hamartomatous pattern
Overlooking neurological or skeletal associations in extensive or facial disease
Underestimating the tendency to recurrent inflammation and secondary infection
Neglecting ophthalmological screening for cataract and anterior-segment anomalies
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Treat the cutaneous naevus with topical keratolytics and retinoids such as tretinoin, or topical vitamin D analogues, to reduce comedonal plugging
Manage inflammatory complications of cysts, abscesses and secondary infection with antibiotics guided by swabs, plus incision and drainage where needed
Consider surgical excision or ablative laser for troublesome or cosmetically distressing lesions
Control associated seizures with antiepileptic drugs and provide developmental support for central nervous system involvement
Manage skeletal anomalies such as scoliosis and limb defects with orthopaedic and physiotherapy input
Arrange ophthalmology review for cataract and other anterior-segment anomalies
Coordinate multidisciplinary dermatology, neurology, orthopaedics and ophthalmology care given the syndromic associations
